note_tweet.text:
Amazon blocked Meta's AI agent last month.
Walmart is giving AI agents their own shopping accounts. With a spending limit.

Three things happened this week that make AI agents actually usable.

—

1. Walmart opened its store to agents

→ Each agent gets its own profile inside your Walmart account
→ You approve every purchase, or set a limit like $50, $100 or $200
→ The agent can't see your card or change how you pay
→ It connects through MCP, not by clicking around the website

Walmart's own line: it's like "adding someone as a cardholder on your credit card."
Profiles roll out within a month. Developers can try the gateway in beta now.

2. 1Password let agents log in without seeing your password

→ The agent asks 1Password to sign in
→ You get an alert and confirm it
→ 1Password fills in the login. The agent never sees it
→ Works with Claude Duet, OpenAI's Dots, Grok Bot, Meta's Muse and more

3. Anthropic and OpenAI gave their agent standards away

→ Anthropic's Agent Skills and OpenAI's Open Responses moved to the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation)
→ They join MCP and AGENTS .MD The foundation now hosts 10 projects

(TechCrunch and The Next Web have the details.)

—

Why this matters if you build:

The hard part of agents was never the model.
It was getting through the door. Logging in, paying, talking to other tools.

This week those doors started opening. Not everywhere. Schwab and JPMorgan still block agents from moving money. Chase says don't give your password to anyone.

My take: the agent that wins won't be the smartest one.
It'll be the one stores, banks and password managers actually let in.
